turns.content: Doctor: Hello—I'm Dr. Agent. I need to ask 3 quick questions: 1) Where exactly is the abdominal pain (and how severe 0–10)? 2) Any fever, vomiting, black/bloody stool, or trouble passing urine? 3) When did the confusion start and is it fluctuating or constant? Doctor: REQUEST TEST: CBC, CMP, LFTs, lipase, urinalysis, lactate, blood glucose. Doctor: REQUEST TEST: CT_Abdomen_Pelvis_with_contrast and CT_Head_wo_contrast.

RESULTS: Temperature 38.9°C (102°F); BP 117/65 mmHg; Heart Rate 110 bpm; Respiratory Rate 19 breaths/min; Oxygen Saturation 95% on room air. Abdominal exam: right upper quadrant discomfort with palpable mass; no visible distension or jaundice; bowel sounds present; normal percussion; no generalized peritonitis. Laboratory: WBC elevated (exact value not provided); liver enzymes, bilirubin not provided. Imaging (abdominal ultrasound): pericholecystic fluid and gallbladder wall thickening without gallstones. Urinalysis, lactate, blood glucose, lipase, CMP/LFTs, CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast, and CT head without contrast: not provided—NORMAL READINGS for missing values.

Doctor: I have one remaining question—are you having worsening confusion or severe right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea/vomiting, and do you feel chills or rigors? Doctor: Given fever, RUQ tenderness with a palpable mass, and ultrasound showing pericholecystic fluid and gallbladder wall thickening (classic for acute cholecystitis), and delirium/AMS likely from systemic infection, my diagnosis is acute calculous or acalculous cholecystitis causing sepsis-related encephalopathy. Doctor: DIAGNOSIS READY: Acute cholecystitis with sepsis-associated delirium/encephalopathy.
